entries.meaning: A false name that someone uses instead of their real one. ---
examples: He checked into the hotel under an alias.
Police say the suspect used at least four aliases.
She published her first book under an alias.

entries.meaning: A feeling of not belonging or of being cut off from other people. ---
examples: The film captures the alienation of a teenager in a new town.
Long remote stretches led to a real sense of alienation from the team.
He writes about alienation in modern city life.

entries.meaning: The state of being in the correct position, or of being in agreement with something else. ---
examples: The front wheels are out of alignment.
There's growing alignment between the two parties on trade.
Check the alignment of the shelves before you screw them in.

entries.meaning: Money that a person pays regularly to a former husband or wife after a divorce. ---
examples: He pays alimony every month until she remarries.
The judge cut his alimony in half after he lost his job.
She receives alimony but no child support.
entries.contrast: Alimony goes to the ex-spouse; money for the children is child support.

entries.meaning: A chemical substance that is the opposite of an acid and turns litmus paper blue. ---
examples: Baking soda is a weak alkali.
Strong alkalis will burn your skin, so wear gloves.
The soil here has too much alkali for blueberries.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A public claim that someone has done something wrong, made before it is proved. ---
examples: The company denies every allegation in the lawsuit.
Allegations of fraud have followed him for years.
The paper printed the allegation without naming a source.

entries.meaning: Loyalty that a person owes to a country, leader, or cause. ---
examples: Students recite the Pledge of Allegiance every morning.
New citizens swear allegiance to the United States.
His allegiance to the old coach never wavered.

entries.meaning: A story in which the characters and events stand for ideas about real life. ---
examples: Animal Farm is an allegory about revolution.
The teacher asked us to find two allegories in the reading.
The whole movie works as an allegory for grief.

entries.meaning: One of the alternative forms of a gene that a person or animal can inherit. ---
examples: You get one allele from each parent.
The allele for blue eyes is recessive.
Researchers linked two alleles to a higher risk of the disease.

entries.meaning: A doctor who specializes in treating allergies. ---
examples: Our pediatrician sent us to an allergist.
The allergist ran a skin test for twenty different foods.
Most allergists in town are booked months out.

entries.meaning: The repeating of the same first sound in words that are close together. ---
examples: "Peter Piper picked a peck" is a classic example of alliteration.
The poem leans hard on alliteration.
Advertisers love alliteration because it sticks in your head.

entries.meaning: An amount of money, time, or resources given to a particular purpose. ---
examples: The department's allocation was cut by ten percent.
Each school gets a separate allocation for supplies.
They reviewed the budget allocations line by line.

entries.meaning: A share or amount of something that is officially given to a person or group. ---
examples: I've already used my allotment of vacation days.
Each family received a small allotment of land.
The office got its monthly allotment of printer paper.
entries.contrast: In British English an allotment is a rented garden plot; Americans use the word for a share or portion.

entries.meaning: A brown spice made from dried berries, used in baking and stews. ---
examples: Add a pinch of allspice to the pumpkin pie filling.
The recipe calls for cinnamon, cloves, and allspice.
I'm out of allspice, so I'll use nutmeg instead.
entries.contrast: Despite the name, allspice is one single spice, not a mix.

entries.meaning: The quality that makes something or someone strongly attractive. ---
examples: The allure of the big city wore off after two winters.
Part of the allure is that the place is so hard to reach.
Old cars have an allure that new ones just don't.

entries.meaning: An indirect reference to something, made without naming it directly. ---
examples: The song is full of allusions to old westerns.
He made an allusion to the argument but never explained it.
The essay traces biblical allusions in her poetry.
entries.contrast: Not the same as illusion (обман зрения): an allusion is a hint or reference.

entries.meaning: A thick-leaved desert plant, or the cooling gel taken from its leaves. ---
examples: Put some aloe on that sunburn.
She keeps an aloe on the kitchen windowsill.
The lotion is mostly water and aloe.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: The habit of staying distant and not mixing with other people. ---
examples: His aloofness at parties is really just shyness.
The new manager's aloofness bothered the whole team.
Cats are famous for their aloofness.

entries.meaning: A medical condition in which a person loses hair from the head or body. ---
examples: She has alopecia and has worn a wig since middle school.
Stress can make alopecia worse.
The doctor diagnosed alopecia after the second round of tests.

entries.meaning: The first letter of the Greek alphabet, often used to mean the first or the strongest. ---
examples: The Greek letter alpha looks a lot like a lowercase a.
The app is still in alpha, so expect bugs.
In a wolf pack, the alpha eats first.

entries.meaning: An informal short word for a graduate of a school or a former member of an organization. ---
examples: She's an alum of the same high school as my brother.
The company hires a lot of alums from that program.
Two alums came back to coach the team.
entries.contrast: Spelled like the chemical alum /ˈæləm/ (AL-uhm, квасцы), but stressed on the second syllable when it means a graduate.

entries.meaning: A mixture of different things combined into one, or the silver material used in tooth fillings. ---
examples: Her style is an amalgam of jazz and country.
The dentist replaced an old amalgam filling.
The neighborhood is an amalgam of old houses and new condos.

entries.meaning: A sweet Italian liqueur that tastes of almonds. ---
examples: He ordered an amaretto sour at the bar.
The cake gets a splash of amaretto in the batter.
There's half a bottle of amaretto left over from Christmas.

entries.meaning: A tall houseplant that grows from a bulb and produces large trumpet-shaped flowers. ---
examples: My aunt gives everyone an amaryllis at Christmas.
The amaryllis on the windowsill finally bloomed.
Two red amaryllises were sitting on the counter in foil pots.

entries.meaning: Someone who does an activity for pleasure rather than as a paid job. ---
examples: He's an amateur, but his photos are better than mine.
The tournament is open to amateurs only.
As a cook I'm a complete amateur.

entries.meaning: A word or statement that can be understood in more than one way. ---
examples: The lawyers found several ambiguities in the contract.
There's an ambiguity in that sentence about who left.
The rules were rewritten to remove an ambiguity.

entries.meaning: The state of having two opposite feelings about something at the same time. ---
examples: There's real ambivalence in the town about the new factory.
She spoke with obvious ambivalence about moving back home.
His ambivalence about the job showed in the interview.

entries.meaning: The food of the gods in Greek myth, or any food that tastes wonderful. ---
examples: In the myths the gods lived on ambrosia and nectar.
After three days of camping food, that burger was ambrosia.
Grandma always brings her ambrosia salad to Thanksgiving.

entries.meaning: A purple stone used in jewelry. ---
examples: Her ring has a small amethyst in the center.
The shop sells raw amethysts by the pound.
February's birthstone is amethyst.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: An instrument that measures electric current in amps. ---
examples: Hook the ammeter up in series with the bulb.
The ammeter on the dashboard showed the battery was draining.
We borrowed two ammeters from the physics lab.

entries.meaning: The coiled fossil shell of a sea animal that died out with the dinosaurs. ---
examples: He found an ammonite in the rocks along the beach.
The museum has a case of polished ammonites.
That spiral fossil is an ammonite, not a snail.

entries.meaning: An official decision to free a group of people from punishment. ---
examples: The government offered an amnesty to anyone who returned a stolen weapon.
Two earlier amnesties had emptied half the prison.
The library holds a late-fee amnesty every August.

entries.meaning: The paying off of a debt in regular equal payments over a set period. ---
examples: The bank sent us an amortization schedule for the mortgage.
Faster amortization means less interest over the life of the loan.
Ask them to explain the amortization before you sign.
entries.contrast: Not the same as Russian амортизация in the sense of shock absorption; this word is only about paying off debt.

entries.meaning: A common antibiotic used to treat ear, throat, and chest infections. ---
examples: The doctor put him on amoxicillin for ten days.
She's allergic to amoxicillin, so they prescribed something else.
Pink liquid amoxicillin is what most American kids get for an ear infection.

entries.meaning: The strength of an electric current, measured in amps. ---
examples: Check the amperage before you plug the heater in.
That circuit can't handle the amperage of a dryer.
The charger has a higher amperage than the old one.

entries.meaning: The size of a wave measured from its middle to its highest point. ---
examples: A louder sound has a greater amplitude.
The graph shows how the amplitude falls off with distance.
The two waves have the same frequency but different amplitudes.

entries.meaning: The surgical removal of an arm, leg, or part of one. ---
examples: The infection was so bad that amputation was the only option.
He learned to walk again six months after the amputation.
The hospital performs dozens of amputations a year.

entries.meaning: A person who has had an arm or leg removed by surgery. ---
examples: He's been an amputee since a motorcycle accident in 2011.
The clinic fits amputees with prosthetic legs.
She's the first amputee to finish the race.

entries.meaning: A small object worn in the belief that it protects against bad luck or harm. ---
examples: He wore a silver amulet on a cord around his neck.
The tomb was full of amulets meant to guard the dead.
She keeps her grandmother's amulet in a drawer.

entries.meaning: A small almond-shaped part of the brain involved in fear and other strong emotions. ---
examples: The amygdala lights up on the scan when subjects see a threat.
Fear starts in the amygdala before you can even think.
The brain has two amygdalae, one on each side.
entries.contrast: Plural is amygdalae (uh-MIG-duh-lee); the g is pronounced.

entries.meaning: Something that belongs to a different time period than the one it appears in. ---
examples: A wristwatch in a Roman movie is an obvious anachronism.
Fax machines are an anachronism in most offices now.
Viewers wrote in about all the anachronisms in the costumes.
entries.contrast: The ch is pronounced /k/: uh-NAK-ruh-niz-uhm.

entries.meaning: A word or phrase made by rearranging the letters of another one. ---
examples: "Listen" is an anagram of "silent."
The puzzle page has three anagrams every Sunday.
His pen name is an anagram of his real name.

entries.meaning: A medicine that reduces pain. ---
examples: Aspirin is a mild analgesic.
The label warns against mixing two analgesics.
She was given a stronger analgesic after surgery.

entries.meaning: A comparison that explains one thing by showing how it is like another. ---
examples: He used an analogy about traffic to explain how the network works.
The analogy breaks down if you push it too far.
The test has a whole section of word analogies.

entries.meaning: A sudden, severe allergic reaction that can make it hard to breathe. ---
examples: Peanuts can cause anaphylaxis in some children.
The school nurse is trained to treat anaphylaxis.
He carries an EpiPen in case of anaphylaxis.

entries.meaning: The political belief that government should be abolished. ---
examples: The course covers socialism, anarchism, and liberalism.
He drifted toward anarchism in his twenties.
Anarchism had a real following among immigrant workers in the 1890s.

entries.meaning: A person who believes that government should be abolished. ---
examples: A group of anarchists marched at the back of the protest.
He called himself an anarchist, but he voted every year.
The bookstore is run by a couple of aging anarchists.

entries.meaning: A situation with no government or no order at all. ---
examples: The city fell into anarchy after the storm.
Without a substitute teacher, third period was pure anarchy.
He warned that cutting the police budget would lead to anarchy.
entries.contrast: The ch is pronounced /k/: AN-er-kee.

entries.meaning: Something a person finds completely unacceptable or hateful. ---
examples: Raising taxes is anathema to that wing of the party.
The very idea of a dress code was anathema to her.
Compromise is anathema to him.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable: uh-NATH-uh-muh.

entries.meaning: The study of the structure of the body, or the structure itself. ---
examples: She's taking anatomy and physiology this semester.
Cats have a very flexible spine, which is unusual anatomy.
The textbook opens with the anatomy of the human heart.

entries.meaning: The family and people a person is descended from. ---
examples: The test said her ancestry was mostly Irish and Polish.
He's proud of his ancestry on his mother's side.
Many families here can trace their ancestry to one small village.

entries.meaning: A robot built to look and move like a human being. ---
examples: The movie is about an android who doesn't know it's a machine.
Two androids serve drinks in the hotel lobby.
The lab is building an android that can climb stairs.

entries.meaning: A short true story about something that happened to someone. ---
examples: He opened the speech with an anecdote about his first job.
The book is a string of anecdotes from her years on the road.
That's an interesting anecdote, but it isn't evidence.
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian анекдот means a joke; an English anecdote is a real little story, usually not funny.

entries.meaning: A garden flower with bright petals and a dark center, or a soft sea creature with waving tentacles. ---
examples: She planted red anemones along the front walk.
A clownfish hides inside a sea anemone.
The anemone closed up as soon as I touched it.
entries.contrast: Stress is on the second syllable: uh-NEM-uh-nee, four syllables.

entries.meaning: A drug that stops a person from feeling pain during surgery or dental work. ---
examples: The dentist gave me a local anesthetic before drilling.
She had a reaction to the anesthetic and woke up nauseous.
Modern anesthetics wear off within a few hours.
entries.contrast: American spelling is anesthetic; the British spelling is anaesthetic.

entries.meaning: A dangerous bulge in the wall of a blood vessel. ---
examples: He died of a brain aneurysm at forty-two.
The scan found a small aneurysm near her heart.
Most aneurysms cause no symptoms until they burst.

entries.meaning: Chest pain caused by the heart not getting enough blood. ---
examples: He gets angina whenever he climbs the stairs too fast.
The pills control her angina pretty well.
Angina is often the first warning sign of heart disease.
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian ангина is a throat infection; English angina is heart-related chest pain.

entries.meaning: A deep feeling of worry and unhappiness about life in general. ---
examples: The album is three quarters teenage angst.
There's a lot of angst in the office about the merger.
He writes about the angst of turning forty.

entries.meaning: Very severe mental or physical pain. ---
examples: You could hear the anguish in her voice.
The family went through months of anguish waiting for news.
He described the anguish of losing the farm.

entries.meaning: A living creature that moves and eats, as opposed to a plant. ---
examples: Wild animals come down to the creek at dusk.
A dolphin is a smart animal.
The farm keeps about forty animals through the winter.

entries.meaning: The technique of making drawings or models appear to move on screen. ---
examples: The animation in that film took four years to finish.
He studied animation at art school.
Hand-drawn animation is rare these days.

entries.meaning: A person who creates moving images for cartoons, films, or games. ---
examples: The studio hired six new animators last month.
She's an animator who works mostly on video games.
The credits list more than two hundred animators.
entries.contrast: In American English an animator draws cartoons; the аниматор who entertains guests at a resort is an entertainer or activities host.

entries.meaning: Japanese animated film and television. ---
examples: My nephew watches nothing but anime.
She got into anime through a friend in high school.
The convention has a whole floor devoted to anime.
entries.contrast: Three syllables, ending in -may: AN-uh-may, not "uh-NEEM".

entries.meaning: Strong dislike or hostility toward someone. ---
examples: There's real animosity between the two coaches.
He left the company without any animosity.
Years of animosity ended with a handshake.

entries.meaning: An atom or group of atoms carrying a negative electric charge. ---
examples: Chloride is an anion.
Anions move toward the positive electrode.
The lab measured the anions dissolved in the water.
entries.contrast: Three syllables, AN-eye-uhn, unlike onion (UN-yuhn).

entries.meaning: A plant whose seeds taste like licorice and are used in cooking. ---
examples: These cookies are flavored with anise.
The sauce has a faint taste of anise.
Anise is what gives that liqueur its licorice flavor.

entries.meaning: The act of one country or city taking over territory and making it part of itself. ---
examples: Congress debated the annexation of Texas for years.
The annexation was condemned by most of the world.
The city council approved two annexations of nearby farmland.

entries.meaning: The complete destruction of something so that nothing is left. ---
examples: The treaty was meant to prevent nuclear annihilation.
The team faced total annihilation in the second half.
He wrote about the annihilation of the forest in a single season.
entries.contrast: The h is silent: uh-nye-uh-LAY-shuhn.

entries.meaning: A note added to a text to explain or comment on part of it. ---
examples: The margins are full of his annotations.
Each annotation explains an unfamiliar word.
She left an annotation on the second paragraph.
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian аннотация means an abstract or summary; an English annotation is a note added to a text.

entries.meaning: A financial product that pays a fixed sum of money every year. ---
examples: He put half his savings into an annuity.
The annuity pays out until she dies.
Some annuities charge very high fees.

entries.meaning: An official ruling that a marriage or contract was never valid. ---
examples: They got an annulment instead of a divorce.
The church granted the annulment two years later.
Annulments are much harder to obtain than divorces.

entries.meaning: The electrode where electric current enters a battery or other device. ---
examples: Connect the red wire to the anode.
The anode in a lithium battery is usually made of graphite.
Both anodes had corroded badly.

entries.meaning: Something that is different from what is normal or expected. ---
examples: The warm February was an anomaly, not a trend.
The software flags anomalies in the payment data.
One bad quarter is an anomaly; three is a pattern.

entries.meaning: The condition of not having your name known. ---
examples: The source spoke on condition of anonymity.
He enjoys the anonymity of a big city.
The app promises complete anonymity.

entries.meaning: An eating disorder in which a person refuses to eat enough and becomes dangerously thin. ---
examples: She was treated for anorexia in her late teens.
Anorexia affects boys as well as girls.
The clinic specializes in anorexia and bulimia.

entries.meaning: A medicine that reduces stomach acid and relieves heartburn. ---
examples: Take an antacid if your stomach still hurts.
There's a bottle of antacids in the glove compartment.
Chewable antacids are sold at every checkout counter.

entries.meaning: Active opposition or hostility between people or groups. ---
examples: There's decades of antagonism between the two towns.
His remarks only added to the antagonism.
The antagonism between the departments slows everything down.

entries.meaning: The small bet each player must put in before a hand of cards is dealt. ---
examples: The ante is a dollar a hand.
Both players threw in their antes.
The new tariffs raised the ante in the trade dispute.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like auntie: AN-tee.

entries.meaning: A long-nosed animal that eats ants and termites with its sticky tongue. ---
examples: The zoo just got a giant anteater.
Anteaters have no teeth at all.
An anteater can eat thousands of ants in a day.

entries.meaning: Something that came before and led to what exists now, or the noun that a pronoun refers back to. ---
examples: In "Maria lost her keys," the antecedent of "her" is Maria.
The movement has antecedents going back to the 1930s.
Every pronoun needs a clear antecedent.

entries.meaning: The part at the top of a flower's stamen that holds the pollen. ---
examples: Cut the anthers off the lilies so they don't stain the tablecloth.
The bee brushed against the anther and picked up pollen.
Label the anthers and the stigma on the diagram.

entries.meaning: A hard, shiny kind of coal that burns with almost no smoke. ---
examples: Eastern Pennsylvania was built on anthracite.
The stove is designed to burn anthracite.
Anthracite gives off more heat than softer coal.

entries.meaning: A serious bacterial disease of cattle and sheep that can also infect people. ---
examples: The herd was vaccinated against anthrax.
Letters containing anthrax were mailed to two senators in 2001.
Anthrax spores can survive in soil for decades.

entries.meaning: A protein made by the immune system to attack a specific germ. ---
examples: The test checks for antibodies in the blood.
Your body makes an antibody for each new infection.
Antibody levels drop over the months after a vaccine.

entries.meaning: A silly or wild bit of behavior meant to get attention. ---
examples: The kids' antics had everyone laughing.
He was suspended for his antics on the field.
Nobody found that last antic funny.
entries.contrast: Almost always used in the plural: antics.

entries.meaning: A disappointing ending that comes after a big build-up. ---
examples: After all that hype, the finale was an anticlimax.
The wedding was fine, but the reception was a real anticlimax.
The season ended in one anticlimax after another.

entries.meaning: A substance that makes the body produce antibodies against it. ---
examples: The rapid antigen test takes fifteen minutes.
A virus carries antigens on its surface.
The vaccine introduces a harmless antigen to train the immune system.

entries.meaning: A main character in a story who lacks the usual heroic qualities. ---
examples: Walter White is television's most famous antihero.
The book's antihero lies to almost everyone.
That decade gave us a whole generation of antiheroes.

entries.meaning: Matter made of particles with the opposite electric charge to ordinary particles. ---
examples: When antimatter meets matter, both are destroyed.
The lab has produced only a few atoms of antimatter.
Half the show's plot runs on antimatter engines.

entries.meaning: A substance that protects cells from damage, found in many fruits and vegetables. ---
examples: Blueberries are loaded with antioxidants.
Vitamin C is a common antioxidant.
The label brags about the antioxidants in the green tea.

entries.meaning: An Italian first course of cured meats, cheeses, olives, and vegetables. ---
examples: We split an antipasto before the pasta came.
She put together an antipasto platter for the party.
There was plenty of antipasto left at the end of the night.

entries.meaning: A drug that fights a virus in the body. ---
examples: The doctor prescribed an antiviral within two days of the first symptoms.
Antivirals work best when you start them early.
There's still no effective antiviral for the common cold.

entries.meaning: A heavy iron block that a blacksmith hammers hot metal on. ---
examples: The blacksmith laid the glowing bar on the anvil.
Old anvils sell for a lot at farm auctions.
In the cartoon, an anvil falls out of the sky.

entries.meaning: A system of laws that keeps racial groups apart and gives one of them all the power. ---
examples: South Africa ended apartheid in the early 1990s.
She grew up under apartheid and later wrote about it.
The museum documents daily life during apartheid.
entries.contrast: The h is silent: say uh-PAR-tayt (or uh-PAR-tite), never uh-PART-hide.

entries.meaning: The opening in a camera lens that lets light through, or any narrow opening. ---
examples: Open the aperture wider if the room is dark.
Both lenses have a maximum aperture of f/1.8.
Light came through a narrow aperture in the wall.

entries.meaning: A short sentence that states a general truth. ---
examples: He ended every lecture with the same aphorism.
The book is a collection of aphorisms about work.
"Less is more" is a famous aphorism.

entries.meaning: A food or drug believed to increase sexual desire. ---
examples: Oysters have a reputation as an aphrodisiac.
None of these so-called aphrodisiacs work.
Power, he joked, is the best aphrodisiac.

entries.meaning: Calm confidence in a difficult situation. ---
examples: She handled the hostile questions with aplomb.
He answered the reporters with surprising aplomb.
The waiter cleaned up the spill with complete aplomb.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: uh-PLAHM.

entries.meaning: A condition in which breathing stops for short periods, usually during sleep. ---
examples: His doctor thinks he has sleep apnea.
The machine treats apnea by keeping the airway open.
Untreated apnea can raise your blood pressure.
entries.contrast: Americans write apnea; the British write apnoea.

entries.meaning: A ghost, or a figure that appears suddenly and strangely. ---
examples: She swore she saw an apparition on the stairs.
The old inn is famous for its apparitions.
In the fog he looked like an apparition.

entries.meaning: The policy of giving in to an aggressive country to avoid a fight. ---
examples: Critics called the deal pure appeasement.
The 1930s taught Europe the cost of appeasement.
He denied that the talks were appeasement.

entries.meaning: A part that sticks out from a larger body, or something added on and less important. ---
examples: A crab uses its front appendages to grab food.
The garage looks like an appendage to the house.
The committee became a useless appendage of the board.

entries.meaning: Cooked apples mashed into a soft, sweet food. ---
examples: The kids eat applesauce with almost everything.
We serve pork chops with applesauce.
You can use applesauce instead of oil in the recipe.
entries.contrast: Applesauce is uncountable: say some applesauce or a jar of applesauce, never an applesauce.

entries.meaning: A small tool used to put a liquid or cream onto something. ---
examples: The polish comes with a foam applicator.
Throw the used applicators in the trash.
Squeeze the tube and spread it with the applicator.

entries.meaning: A person who has been given a job or position by someone in power. ---
examples: The governor's newest appointee takes office Monday.
Several appointees resigned after the scandal.
He was a political appointee, not a career official.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is to decide what property is worth. ---
examples: The bank sent an appraiser to look at the house.
Two appraisers came up with very different numbers.
She works as an appraiser for an insurance company.

entries.meaning: A feeling of worry that something bad is about to happen. ---
examples: She opened the letter with some apprehension.
There is real apprehension about the layoffs.
He watched the storm approach with growing apprehension.

entries.meaning: A way of dealing with a problem or a task. ---
examples: Her approach to teaching is very hands-on.
We tried three different approaches before one worked.
The company needs a fresh approach to hiring.

entries.meaning: Official permission, or the feeling that something is good. ---
examples: The plan still needs approval from the city council.
He looked at his father for approval.
The drug won federal approval last spring.

entries.meaning: A natural ability to learn or do something well. ---
examples: She has a real aptitude for languages.
The school gives an aptitude test in ninth grade.
The job matches his aptitudes almost perfectly.
entries.contrast: Americans say AP-tih-tood; the British add a y sound: AP-tih-tyood.

entries.meaning: A bridge or channel built to carry water over a long distance. ---
examples: A Roman aqueduct still stands outside the town.
The city gets its water through a hundred-mile aqueduct.
Several aqueducts were damaged in the earthquake.

entries.meaning: A layer of rock or sand underground that holds water. ---
examples: Farmers here pump water from a deep aquifer.
The aquifer is dropping about a foot a year.
Fertilizer runoff has polluted two aquifers.

entries.meaning: A person or body with the power to settle a dispute or decide what is correct. ---
examples: The court is the final arbiter of the Constitution.
Magazines used to be the arbiters of taste.
Both sides agreed to accept the arbiter's decision.

entries.meaning: Buying something in one market and selling it in another to profit from the price difference. ---
examples: The fund made most of its money on arbitrage.
Fast computers have squeezed the profit out of arbitrage.
He spent ten years doing currency arbitrage.
entries.contrast: The ending sounds French — AR-bih-trahzh — not like the -age in garbage.

entries.meaning: An angel of the highest rank. ---
examples: The painting shows an archangel with a sword.
Michael and Gabriel are the best-known archangels.
A stone archangel stands over the church door.
entries.contrast: Here ch sounds like k — ARK-ayn-jul — but in archbishop and archer it is the ch of church.

entries.meaning: A bishop of the highest rank, in charge of a large church region. ---
examples: The archbishop spoke at the memorial service.
Two archbishops signed the open letter.
He was named archbishop of Chicago in March.

entries.meaning: Someone who shoots with a bow and arrows. ---
examples: The archer hit the center of the target twice.
Medieval archers could fire ten arrows a minute.
She's the best archer on the college team.

entries.meaning: A collection of old documents or records, or the place where they are kept. ---
examples: The letters are in the university archive.
He spent a week in the city archives.
The newspaper put its whole archive online.
entries.contrast: The ch sounds like k: AR-kyve.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is to look after historical records. ---

examples: After the layoff, she became the family's only breadwinner.
In many households both parents are breadwinners.
He felt the pressure of being the breadwinner at twenty-three.

entries.meaning: Damage caused by things being broken, or the amount of such damage. ---
examples: The shipping insurance covers breakage in transit.
Wrap each glass separately to prevent breakage.
The store loses about two percent a year to breakage.

entries.meaning: An important discovery or advance that solves a stubborn problem. ---
examples: The vaccine was a major breakthrough in public health.
After months of therapy she finally had a breakthrough.
The lab has reported two breakthroughs this year.

entries.meaning: A swimming stroke in which the arms sweep forward and the legs kick like a frog's. ---
examples: She swims the breaststroke faster than anyone on the team.
He won gold in the 100-meter breaststroke.
The class covers freestyle, backstroke, and breaststroke.
entries.contrast: The first part rhymes with rest: BREST-strohk, not 'breest'.

entries.meaning: The act of taking air into the lungs and letting it out. ---
examples: Her breathing got slower as she fell asleep.
The nurse checked his pulse and breathing.
Deep breathing helps me calm down before a test.
entries.contrast: Long ee with a voiced th: BREE-thing. The noun breath is short and hissed: /brɛθ/, BRETH.

entries.meaning: Short trousers that fasten just below the knee, worn for riding or in period costume. ---
examples: The riders wore white breeches and black boots.
His costume included a wig and velvet breeches.
A pair of leather breeches hung by the stable door.
entries.contrast: Said BRICH-iz, not 'breech-ez'. Always plural, like pants — a pair of breeches.

entries.meaning: Shortness, especially of speech or writing. ---
examples: For the sake of brevity, I'll skip the background.
The memo was admired for its brevity.
Brevity is the soul of wit.

entries.meaning: A person or company that makes beer. ---
examples: He worked as a brewer in Portland for ten years.
The country's largest brewer is raising prices again.
Local brewers set up tents along the river.

entries.meaning: A bar or restaurant that brews its own beer on the premises. ---
examples: There's a new brewpub on Third Street.
We had burgers at a brewpub downtown.
The town has three brewpubs within a few blocks.

entries.meaning: A prickly bush, or one of its thorny stems. ---
examples: The dog came back with briars stuck in its fur.
A thick briar had grown across the trail.
We cut back the briars along the fence line.
entries.contrast: Also spelled brier; both are said BRY-ur.

entries.meaning: A worker who builds walls and other structures out of bricks. ---
examples: His grandfather was a bricklayer in Chicago.
The contractor hired two more bricklayers for the job.
A good bricklayer can set hundreds of bricks a day.

entries.meaning: A soft, mild French cheese with a white rind. ---
examples: She served brie with crackers and green apples.
Warm the brie in the oven for ten minutes.
There's half a wheel of brie left in the fridge.

entries.meaning: Short, close-fitting underpants with no legs. ---
examples: He bought a three-pack of cotton briefs.
The store sells boxers, briefs, and boxer briefs.
A clean pair of briefs was all he had left in the bag.
entries.contrast: Always plural, like pants: a pair of briefs, never 'a brief' in this sense.

entries.meaning: Great brightness, or unusually great intelligence and skill. ---
examples: No one doubted the brilliance of her argument.
The brilliance of the stage lights made him squint.
There are flashes of brilliance in his early work.

entries.meaning: The very edge of something, especially of a dangerous situation. ---
examples: The company was on the brink of bankruptcy.
They pulled back from the brink at the last minute.
She stood at the brink of the canyon and looked down.

entries.meaning: The tactic of pushing a dangerous situation to the edge to force the other side to give in. ---
examples: The budget fight was another round of brinkmanship.
Voters are tired of brinkmanship over the debt ceiling.
His brinkmanship nearly wrecked the negotiations.

entries.meaning: A light, sweet French bread made with butter and eggs. ---
examples: The burger comes on a brioche bun.
She picked up two brioches at the bakery.
French toast is best made with day-old brioche.

entries.meaning: A small block of pressed charcoal or coal used as fuel. ---
examples: Pile the briquettes in a pyramid before lighting them.
One bag of briquettes lasts us the whole summer.
Wait until the briquettes turn gray before you start grilling.

entries.meaning: The business or activity of sending out programs on radio and television. ---
examples: She studied broadcasting at Northwestern.
Public broadcasting depends on donations from viewers.
He spent forty years in broadcasting.

entries.meaning: A firm that buys and sells stocks, property, or insurance for clients. ---
examples: He opened an account at an online brokerage.
Several brokerages cut their price targets for the stock.
The brokerage charges no fee for stock trades.

entries.meaning: A wild or half-tamed horse of the American West. ---
examples: He was thrown by a bronco at the rodeo.
The ranch still breaks broncos the old way.
Riding a bucking bronco takes eight seconds of nerve.

entries.meaning: The long handle of a broom, or the whole broom a witch is imagined riding. ---
examples: The witch costume came with a plastic broomstick.
He propped the door open with a broomstick.
Kids raced around the yard on broomsticks.

entries.meaning: A feeling of closeness among people, or an organized group whose members treat one another as brothers. ---
examples: The team was held together by a real sense of brotherhood.
His father belonged to a railroad workers' brotherhood.
Several brotherhoods marched together in the parade.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: A small square of dense, chewy chocolate cake. ---
examples: She brought a pan of brownies to the potluck.
I'll take a brownie and a glass of milk.
These brownies are still warm from the oven.

entries.meaning: The heaviest part of something bad, such as an attack or a storm. ---
examples: Coastal towns took the brunt of the hurricane.
Younger workers bore the brunt of the layoffs.
She took the brunt of her boss's anger.

entries.meaning: Cruel, violent treatment of people. ---
examples: The report documents police brutality in several cities.
He described the brutality of the prison camp.
The film does not hide the brutality of the war.

entries.meaning: A grain-like seed used for flour and porridge, and the plant it comes from. ---
examples: Sunday mornings we make buckwheat pancakes.
The field behind the barn is planted with buckwheat.
Soba noodles are made from buckwheat flour.

entries.meaning: Someone who knows a lot about a subject and follows it as a hobby. ---
examples: My uncle is a Civil War buff.
Film buffs will recognize the reference right away.
You don't have to be a wine buff to enjoy this bottle.

entries.meaning: Something placed between two things to soften the effect of one on the other. ---
examples: Savings act as a buffer against unexpected bills.
A row of trees serves as a buffer between the road and the houses.
The agreement created a buffer zone along the border.

entries.meaning: A small light vehicle, such as a horse-drawn carriage or an open off-road car. ---
examples: An Amish buggy was moving slowly down the shoulder.
They rented a dune buggy for the afternoon.
Two buggies were parked outside the general store.

entries.meaning: A small brass horn with no valves, used to sound military signals. ---
examples: A bugle played Taps at the graveside.
Camp started every morning with a bugle.
The museum has two Civil War bugles on display.

entries.meaning: Cracked wheat that has been steamed and dried, used in salads and side dishes. ---
examples: Tabbouleh is made with bulgur, parsley, and lemon.
Soak the bulgur in hot water for twenty minutes.
We keep bulgur and couscous in the pantry.

entries.meaning: An eating disorder in which a person overeats and then vomits or otherwise avoids gaining weight. ---
examples: She was treated for bulimia in college.
Bulimia often goes unnoticed for years.
The clinic specializes in anorexia and bulimia.

entries.meaning: A public event in which a matador fights and usually kills a bull. ---
examples: We went to a bullfight in Seville.
Tickets to the bullfight sold out in a day.
Bullfights are banned in some Spanish regions.

entries.meaning: The sport or tradition of fighting bulls in an arena. ---
examples: Bullfighting has lost popularity with younger Spaniards.
Animal rights groups campaign against bullfighting.
He wrote a whole book about bullfighting.

entries.meaning: Gold or silver in the form of bars, valued by weight. ---
examples: The vault holds several tons of gold bullion.
Investors have been buying silver bullion all year.
The coins sell at the bullion price plus a small fee.
entries.contrast: Not bouillon /ˈbuːjɑːn/ (BOO-yahn), which is broth.

entries.meaning: Nonsense or lies — a very common but vulgar word. ---
examples: His excuse was complete bullshit.
I'm tired of listening to corporate bullshit.
She called bullshit on the whole story.
entries.contrast: Vulgar. Fine among friends, never in class, an interview, or writing for work.

entries.meaning: Someone who repeatedly frightens or hurts weaker people. ---
examples: A bully on the bus took his lunch money.
Most bullies back down when you stand up to them.
She refused to let a bully run her classroom.

entries.meaning: Repeated cruel treatment of someone weaker, especially at school or work. ---
examples: The school has a strict policy on bullying.
Online bullying follows kids home now.
She reported the bullying to her manager.

entries.meaning: An informal word for a disappointing or annoying situation. ---
examples: Rain on your birthday — what a bummer.
It's a bummer that the concert got canceled.
The flat tire was the first of several bummers that day.

entries.meaning: A thick elastic cord, used to strap down loads or to jump from a height. ---
examples: He strapped the cooler down with a bungee.
She went bungee jumping in New Zealand.
A pack of bungees costs about ten dollars.

entries.meaning: A painful swollen bump at the base of the big toe. ---
examples: Tight shoes made her bunion worse.
He had surgery on both bunions last spring.
The podiatrist said the bunion was hereditary.
entries.русский: шишка (косточка) у основания большого пальца ноги

entries.meaning: In baseball, a hit made by holding the bat still so the ball rolls a short distance. ---
examples: He laid down a perfect bunt to move the runner over.
The third baseman charged in to field the bunt.
Two bunts in a row caught the defense off guard.

entries.meaning: The ability of an object to float, or the upward push a liquid gives it. ---
examples: Salt water gives swimmers extra buoyancy.
The vest adds enough buoyancy to keep a child afloat.
We measured the buoyancy of each block in the tank.

entries.meaning: A heavy load, or a difficult duty or worry someone has to carry. ---
examples: Caring for both parents became a real burden.
The new tax shifts the burden onto small businesses.
He carried the burden of the secret for years.

entries.meaning: A style of stage entertainment mixing comedy, song, and striptease. ---
examples: The theater started out as a burlesque house in the 1920s.
She performs burlesque on weekends.
The show is a modern take on old-fashioned burlesque.

entries.meaning: A loose garment worn by some Muslim women that covers the whole body and face. ---
examples: Several countries have banned the burqa in public buildings.
She wore a blue burqa in the photograph.
The rules on burqas vary from region to region.

entries.meaning: A sudden short outbreak of sound, energy, or activity. ---
examples: There was a burst of applause when she finished.
He works in short bursts and then takes a break.
A burst of wind knocked the umbrella over.

entries.meaning: A man who works in business, especially at a senior level. ---
examples: Her father was a businessman who traveled constantly.
Two businessmen were arguing in the hotel lobby.
He presents himself as a self-made businessman.
entries.contrast: The plural businessmen is said BIZ-nis-men. Use businessperson when the gender is unknown.

entries.meaning: Noisy, busy movement of people in a place. ---
examples: I miss the bustle of the city.
The kitchen was full of bustle an hour before service.
They wanted a quiet town away from all the bustle.
entries.contrast: The t is silent: BUS-uhl, like hustle and whistle.

entries.meaning: Someone who is too interested in other people's private affairs. ---
examples: The neighborhood busybody watches everyone's driveway.
Don't be such a busybody.
A couple of busybodies had already called the police.
entries.русский: назойливый человек, любитель совать нос в чужие дела

entries.meaning: Tasks given to keep people occupied rather than to accomplish anything. ---
examples: The substitute handed out busywork all afternoon.
Most of my first week was busywork.
Cut the busywork and let the team do real work.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is cutting up and selling meat. ---
examples: Ask the butcher to trim the fat off.
There's a good butcher two blocks over.
The butchers start work at four in the morning.

entries.meaning: The chief male servant of a large household. ---
examples: The butler answered the door.
In the movie, the butler did it.
The estate once employed two butlers and a cook.

entries.meaning: An informal word for the part of the body you sit on. ---
examples: Get off your butt and help me.
He slipped on the ice and landed on his butt.
The jeans were too tight in the butt.

entries.meaning: A steep, isolated hill with a flat top, common in the American West. ---
examples: A red butte rose out of the desert ahead of us.
We camped at the base of the butte.
The highway runs between two sandstone buttes.
entries.contrast: Rhymes with cute: BYOOT, not like butt.

entries.meaning: A small wild plant with shiny yellow cup-shaped flowers. ---
examples: The field was covered in buttercups.
She tucked a buttercup behind her ear.
Buttercups come up every May along the ditch.

entries.meaning: A sweet flavor or candy made from butter and brown sugar. ---
examples: He ordered the sundae with butterscotch sauce.
There's a bowl of butterscotch candies by the register.
The pudding tastes like butterscotch.

entries.meaning: A low humming sound, or excited talk about something new. ---
examples: There's a lot of buzz about her new album.
I heard a buzz and found a wasp at the window.
The refrigerator makes strange buzzes at night.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: An electric device that makes a buzzing sound as a signal. ---
examples: Press the buzzer and I'll let you in.
He scored right before the buzzer.
The contestants each have a buzzer in front of them.

entries.meaning: A fashionable word or phrase used to sound impressive, often with little real meaning. ---
examples: Synergy is the buzzword everyone hates.
His presentation was nothing but buzzwords.
Every year a new buzzword takes over the industry.

entries.meaning: A rule a club, company, or association makes to govern itself.
examples: The homeowners' association changed its bylaws last year.
That's against the club's bylaws.
A bylaw requires two weeks' notice before any vote.
